[h1]Decide the fate of citizens of the world in this surveillance thriller![/h1]

You start the game by creating your character. Only gripe I have here is that there aren’t many choices as far as looks goes. It’d be nice to have more than one face type for the male and female. After that, you go through a very detailed tutorial that goes through the basics of what it will take to get you through the job you’ll be tasked with.

The game is deals with a story that’s shaped by your choices as you completed various assignments, gather evidence, flex your powers, and gather profiles. You don’t have to snoop either. As you progress through the game, you’ll have various choices that will allow you to take a stand against the very government organization you work for. A regular in-game cyber revolutionary. 

However, doing more for your boss means a higher clearance level and a higher clearance level means unlocking cooler (albeit creepier) powers, once classified information, lots more money and of course, prestige. With a higher salary, you can impress or intimidate your peers with purchases like new homes and more.

The game play is slow, but goes as fast as you want it to. I mean that in the sense that if you’re the type like me that combs through evidence and meticulously pieces together a person's profile, this will be the game for you. The main story clues are littered throughout your missions. So keep your eyes peeled. 

The music fits the narrative and the UI is clean. The developers are constantly listening and are active on the Steam Discussions. So, if there is a bug you come across, post to the Discussions and you can be sure a developer will take your problem into account. The only bug I came across was the weird save bug where my game would not save, but after a few updates, the saves are working.

I backed the game, but it's $14.99 and runs about 8-10 if you’re not rushing through it. You can definitely stretch that time out by investigating and going through the side content of which there’s a good amount of. The developers have said they plan on adding more content after the game’s ending and that you will be able to continue after your end of game save.

I recommend Need to Know: The Mass Surveillance Thriller Game. If you enjoy intrigue, espionage, and tools at your fingertips for finding out people’s secrets, then this game is for you. It’s a slow burn that works your detective skills and you can be either for or against the government. The game still has a few bugs, but the developers are quickly churning out updates and changelogs that address concerns.

In a nutshell: A good game, with some great ideas, that needs some polish on the execution, with a number of technical and interface issues that drag down a good story and a great idea.

Put simply, the idea of a game where you move through the hierarchy of a sinister spying agency is a great one, and this game's greatest success so far in my time with it has been not only showing how quickly the power to snoop on everything and everyone can go wrong, but also, and crucially, how it can still also be a force for good. The story is I think the strongest point of the game for me, because it's depiction of the ironically named 'Department of Liberty' is not really as some cartoon villain 'Illuminati conspiracy' but as a government organisation set up in response to a great crisis which, at least initially, is comprised largely of ordinary people. Sure, some of the people you meet in the game are dubiously motivated at best, but the game reinforces in the narrative consistently that there are good people in the DoL, who genuinely believe the spying they engage in is justified and indeed, there are examples in game where the power you use does make a real difference.

I can't say much more without spoiling the hell out of the game, but suffice it to say, if story is what you want, the game offers an intriguing story, and while it may not be a Tom Clancy tale, I've found it engaging and compelling.

Likewise, the gameplay offers good challenge, requiring you to carefully dissect the data you sift through, looking not just for keywords early on but as time goes on, looking for more complicated and easily missed details, like tracing suspicious bank activity with logs of suspicious contacts, and working out if they match up or are a red herring. These shifting challenges do a reasonably good job of building on each other, with each clearance level you go through iterating on previous challenges with an extra layer of complexity, and this organic growth of difficulty is largely well-executed. But it does lead into the big problem in the game: communication.

This game has a real problem communicating with the player, and I think it's largely down to an interface that can be clunky and unintuitive. Partially this is down to bugs, like notifications on your phone not displaying so you're left staring blankly waiting for something to happen, to more egregious errors like typos in the keywords you're looking for, and contextual menus being hard to close once opened and obscuring the screen. These are all fixable issues thankfully, and while irritating, they don't for me drag the game down too much, but the sooner they are resolved, the better, and they are likely to irritate some players too much to continue.

Also, the game can be ambiguous in what the objectives of each day actually require. For instance, you might be asked to look for keywords, but the game isn't good at indicating whether you need a literal, case-sensitive match of the word, or a contextual match. For instance, if the keyword was 'Bomb Kit' and you saw a log that said 'making my own bombs in a kit', you might well flag that as suspicious, and logically, it totally is, but because the game is looking for a case-sensitive, exact match, it marks you down as wrong for it. Again, these issues are not exactly common, but they're infrequent enough to annoy, and for me are the biggest issue of all in the game, but again, can be fixed by the devs.

So in the end, I recommend this game, but I do it with an advisory: if you want a good story, with fun challenges and an engaging concept of government intelligence and the morality of that, then I highly recommend it, but make sure you go in right now knowing there are currently technical and design issues, and while these will likely be fixed, as of the time of this review they exist, and they can annoy. Hopefully you'll be like me, and able to see through the roughness to the diamond within, and enjoy the experience for what it is, not what you necessarily would like it to be.

Very fun game that does an excellent job of portraying the slippery slope when dealing with the question of rights vs security.

*** Spoilers ***
You start off with basic tasks like hunting down murderers or catching terrorists, but then a hurricane hits...

... And you're not permitted to go snooping through people's offline data, but you break the law anyway because if you can track them down, you can send FEMA their location and save some lives! So it's fine, right? Sure, some people lose a bit of privacy, but you're rescuing them from the hurricane!

And then as you rise through the ranks you get a bit more power and you start dealing with tracking down serial killers or stopping an active shooter... But then a senator doesn't like the fact that your department is ignoring people's rights to privacy and wants to shut you down...

... So you blackmail her by digging through her data and finding embarassing information to damage her career. Can't have her foolish ideals stand in the way, obstructing your quest to save lives, right?

And then a bunch of corporations give you access to their data, making your job to track down terrorists even easier, and helping you along the way in your original mission to find a man who caused a few nuclear reactors to overload in a massive terrorist attack, but they want a couple favours...

... So you start doing a bit of corporate espionage on the side, but it's fine, I'm sure, because the backroom deals are how you make progress, and no one *really* needs to keep their shopping history private, do they?

But then some of this stuff gets leaked and more politicians start rallying against it. Fools. They don't know how hard you're working to keep this country safe! They don't know how necessary it is to use this data...

... So you launch a disinformation campaign to silence them and ruin their credibility. It was their fault anyways. They threatened the department, and you needed to protect it! You're the only one standing in the way of the terrorists attacking america, so getting your hands dirty sometimes is fine if it's to protect the greater good, right?

So throughout the game you're doing these underhanded deals, blackmail and character assassinations, but it's fine because you're catching terrorists, saving lives, and generally making sure the citizens can go on with their happy little lives. Soon it pays off! You catch a terrorist who leads you to a terrorist who leads you to a whole network of them! ... but they're scattered across the globe, and many of the countries aren't too keen on sending them to the states for judgement...

... Well they stand in your way! They're harbouring enemies of the state, that's basically an act of war, right? You need to show these governments the errors of their ways... Or maybe you can't. Maybe you should arm some of the militant groups in the countries who are more friendly towards US interests... So you start distributing arms to them and help them seize power, but it's fine, right? You toppled a government and installed a few dictatorships, but you've got to help your country! They were basically asking for it anyways by hiding your enemies, right? So what if a few thousand people on the otherside of the world got killed, you're supposed to protect Americans and that's what you're going to do!

But now your powers are growing and word of your department's actions are reaching the journalists, who are writing scathing criticisms of you and turning the people against you... Well you can't have that happen, so you need to silence them, either by getting them fired or threatening them to keep quiet! Freedom of speech is just getting in the way here, this sacrifice is for the good of the nation, right? Right?!

Despite your best efforts public opinion is still slowly turning against you, and the politicians are noticing... well there's an election coming up, so you've got to make sure a politician friendly to your department gets in. Can't have the president disband the department of liberty, there's still so much work left to do! 

... So you blackmail politicians, leak incriminating documents, and funnel support towards your prefered candidate, ensuring she wins the election. You've subverted democracy but it's fine, right? You need to protect the department because it protects the nation! You're the hero of this story after all! You can't let people who don't understand get in the way, right guys? Right?! Sacrifices must be made! It's for the good of the nation! The good of us all! There's no way I could be the villain, right?! I am the hero here!!!!

But of course, it doesn't stop there. You need more power. Even when you're launching military assaults on embassies in foreign nations, even when you drone-strike your own citizens, even when you assassinate the leaders of other countries who once tried to help you but now stand in your way... 

And then you see it. You get betrayed. People want the power your department has, and your boss and other corporations are vying for the systems that now control the world. What was a perfect, all-seeing system is being used as a pawn by people for petty power plays and revenge... to further their own ideals at the expense of everyone else. You know that you need to end this. You need to stop it. The people at the top need to be brought down. A system this powerful can't remain in the hands of those who would abuse it. A system this perfect either needs to be destroyed or to remain under the control of someone who would use it for good... someone like you... And after all, you're the hero, so why not take it? It's for the good of the nation after all... 

*** End Spoilers ***

Unfortunately there's still a few problems with the game. The interface is not nearly as responsive as it should be for as simple a game as this is. Additionally when you get assignments cross-referencing between multiple suspects,... ugh... the limitations of the UI really make themselves known, and despite there being hundreds of HCI papers out there for how to build proper interfaces when comparing data, this game chooses to use none of them. As someone who worked in an Info-vis lab for a while, I can safely say that the method they chose to link data between two different suspects is one of the most annoying and tedious ways they could have possibly done it. You will audiably groan when you see the mission rules "Link evidence when two suspects travel to the same city at the same time.". It is that bad. Fortunately these missions are few and far between, so you don't have to deal with it too often.

I also didn't like that your actions basically had no lasting effects. Any big choice either ends the game or lets you continue playing. I was really hoping that...

*** Spoilers ***
When you get betrayed, you would have a chance to work with the Snow Owl black-ops division instead of with Tripwire to work your way back up to the top. Maybe based on which faction you had a higher reputation with. They're black-ops anyways, with everything they do being classified and deniable, so helping you wouldn't be completely out of the question.
*** End Spoilers ***

That aside, the game was very fun and very satisfying to play. It played around with a lot of neat ideas, and again, I really liked the story. I also liked how it showed your progression from living in a trashy apartment and working in basically a basement closet to living in a super upscale neighbourhood and leading your own division as you progress through the ranks. I highly recommend it.

8/10

review_text_raw: A very meh take on the spying/censorship genre. You play as a secret government agent who scans people's private data looking for criminals. The data you get to scan is reasonably diverse and requires attention, but the tone and presentation are just underwhelming. The game makes weak attempts to make you feel uneasy because you invade the privacy of your friends — introduced so poorly, I didn't even notice a character's name was similar to one in my contact list because I've only had a whopping one conversation with them before. Also, a game this simple has no right to run so poorly as to stutter.

[quote]Edit Saturday, November 3, 2018:
As a Monomyth developer posted below this review, this game has changed a lot since it's release and since I wrote this review. While I do not currently have time to give the game another shot due to classes, keep in mind that the review below is not an accurate reflection of the current version of Need to Know.
[/quote]

So I tried to like this game, I really did, and I was one of the ones who followed the hype from the first trailer release in the Kickstarter campaign. I really looked forward to the Papers, Please -eqsue surveillance game that the trailers advertised. Holding out to release (remember, no pre-orders!), however, revealed some key flaws that the game has.

[h1]Lack of Tutorial[/h1]
The lack of a tutorial is my primary issue with Need to Know. With almost zero instruction given, the player has no clue on how to progress, how to use the different tools provided in-game, and what distinguishes a subject between a "safe" individual and a threat. Players are expected to know beforehand what all the tools do and how to use them effectively, and  with the game not arming the players with that knowledge, I and many others were left confused as to what to do almost constantly.

[h1]User Interface[/h1]
The current user interface is extremely similar to the user interface that was advertised throughout the developer cycle. While it seems to be extremely sleek and inviting, don't let its looks fool you. The UI was another primary issue with Need to Know. In practice, the UI was sluggish and huge on-screen, with every single element in each window being blown up unnecessarily. Everything except any back or close indicators, which took minutes to find on several occasions. In the beginning of the game, it even took me about 10 minutes to figure out how to begin the first mission! 

[h1]Final Evidence is not consistent with Evidence Requirements[/h1]
At the beginning of each mission, you are given specific key evidence to look out for while analyzing individuals. Several times, the evidence the game wanted me to find were inconsistent with the requirements it gave me. This meant I often “missed” evidence which was never actually listed as a requirement.

[h1]Inconsistent Results after Missions[/h1]
As part of the story, you need to build up your agency's trust in you by successfully analyzing, identifying key elements a suspect might exhibit, and eventually classifying the subject as safe or a threat. These trust points given, however, were often inconsistent. Successfully classify and identify all pieces of evidence in a mission? Have 15 trust points! Missed one piece of evidence? There goes 30 points!

[h1]Inconsistent Dialogue[/h1]
Have a bad day and lose a lot of trust points? Doesn't matter, your boss will let you know what a great job you did today!

[h1]Bugs and Glitches[/h1]
While many people (such as myself) disregard the bug warnings in games and play them anyway only to still have a positive experience, let me tell you that it is not the case with this game. Throughout playing, I experienced numerous bugs, some of which were game breaking or needed a restart. For example, after losing in the prologue (why is that even possible?) and making a new profile the game glitched out and showed two different points in the story, progressing through them simultaneously, requiring a full restart of the game and clearing out the old profile and creating a new profile. Notifications on your in-game phone often appear and disappear in under a second, not giving you enough time to read what it says. You can’t even change the wallpaper.

[h1]In Conclusion[/h1]
In its current state, I cannot recommend Need to Know. The game has vital problems that it needs to solve, problems so important that it makes you wonder if Monomyth Games even play-tested all the features in-game before the final release, in despite of several beta versions being released to Kickstarter backers in the previous months. The game feels like a rushed beta version, even though the game was delayed by a month. Should Monomyth Games fix these key issues, I would gladly re-purchase the game for another shot at Need to Know.

Players are expected to know beforehand what all the tools do and how to use them effectively, and with the game not arming the players with that knowledge, I and many others were left confused as to what to do almost constantly. [h1]User Interface[/h1] The current user interface is extremely similar to the user interface that was advertised throughout the developer cycle. While it seems to be extremely sleek and inviting, don't let its looks fool you. The UI was another primary issue with Need to Know. In practice, the UI was sluggish and huge on-screen, with every single element in each window being blown up unnecessarily. Everything except any back or close indicators, which took minutes to find on several occasions. In the beginning of the game, it even took me about 10 minutes to figure out how to begin the first mission! [h1]Final Evidence is not consistent with Evidence Requirements[/h1] At the beginning of each mission, you are given specific key evidence to look out for while analyzing individuals. Several times, the evidence the game wanted me to find were inconsistent with the requirements it gave me. This meant I often “missed” evidence which was never actually listed as a requirement. [h1]Inconsistent Results after Missions[/h1] As part of the story, you need to build up your agency's trust in you by successfully analyzing, identifying key elements a suspect might exhibit, and eventually classifying the subject as safe or a threat. These trust points given, however, were often inconsistent. Successfully classify and identify all pieces of evidence in a mission? Have 15 trust points! Missed one piece of evidence? There goes 30 points! [h1]Inconsistent Dialogue[/h1] Have a bad day and lose a lot of trust points? Doesn't matter, your boss will let you know what a great job you did today! [h1]Bugs and Glitches[/h1] While many people (such as myself) disregard the bug warnings in games and play them anyway only to still have a positive experience, let me tell you that it is not the case with this game. Throughout playing, I experienced numerous bugs, some of which were game breaking or needed a restart. For example, after losing in the prologue (why is that even possible?) and making a new profile the game glitched out and showed two different points in the story, progressing through them simultaneously, requiring a full restart of the game and clearing out the old profile and creating a new profile. Notifications on your in-game phone often appear and disappear in under a second, not giving you enough time to read what it says. You can’t even change the wallpaper. [h1]In Conclusion[/h1] In its current state, I cannot recommend Need to Know. The game has vital problems that it needs to solve, problems so important that it makes you wonder if Monomyth Games even play-tested all the features in-game before the final release, in despite of several beta versions being released to Kickstarter backers in the previous months. The game feels like a rushed beta version, even though the game was delayed by a month. Should Monomyth Games fix these key issues, I would gladly re-purchase the game for another shot at Need to Know.

The game description says: "You must spy on people’s deepest secrets, pick apart their private lives, and determine how dangerous they are. You can also resist these suffocating privacy invasions by aiding underground groups in leaking data to the media. Or, you can just use all of that juicy classified information for your own personal gain. Your call."

I took this statement literally, and after my first major 'choice', I was told I failed and the game returned to the menu screen.

Now don't get me wrong. I have no problem with fail conditions in games, or even perma-death consquences to actions, but this fail condition was so illogical that it is [i]exceptionally[/i] unique amongst my experiences with video games and choice-driven RPGs. It went like this:

[spoiler]Civilian privacy protection group (TripWire) asks me to sell classified data to them instead of to an internal operative within the department itself. When they ask, I refuse.

Nevermind what you tell them, the game adds them to your buyer list anyway and assigns them a relationship meter. 

When I don't sell data to them the very first time I have the opportunity, and the relationship meter reaches 0, I get this text at the game-over screen:

"TripWire became dissatisfied with your lack of assistance and notified the Department. You have been arrested for treason."

Arrested for treason....for [i]not[/i] selling classified government data to an outside group.[/spoiler]

Choice is expressly offered in the game description, but the choices are pointless when they merely determine [i]if[/i] you can continue instead of [i]how[/i] you continue.

Couple this with a lot of bugs, lack of tutorial and cluttered, clunky UI, and I simply can't recommend it in it's current state.

The game shows promise, but it needs polishing.

Well, I certainly have some thoughts about this game after beating it. Let’s get through them starting with the positives.

- The soundtrack is great! It adds to the intensity and urgency during some missions and very much fits with the whole mass surveillance theme. 
- Some missions were very good and fun. Definitely some memorable ones especially when you got better clearance levels. (As long as they weren’t crossmatch missions which I’ll get to in a bit) 

And that’s about it with the positives :/ on to the negatives which overall, lead me to not recommend this game especially if you respect your time.

- Bad tutorials. One of the biggest problems with the game. The guide talks pretty fast and the dialogue during its explanations keeps going rather than clicking to proceed which can make you easily miss information on what to do. Often times I felt like I was thrown into a pool expecting to know how to swim. This was especially the case with what I think is the worst mission type in the game, crossmatch. I was just lost with these missions and just rushed through them. I saw in a couple of cases I could just approve everyone very quickly and my performance would still be good.
- Money is useless. All you can do with your hard earned cash is spending it on items for your house that serve no purpose other than just sitting there. [spoiler] (Near the end of the game, you go to prison and are on the run after escaping which further adds to the uselessness of money and items from the shop.)[/spoiler] You never have to pay rent other than one point in the game but you can easily do something to not pay. Other similar games like Not Tonight, papers please etc had much better economies and it would’ve been nice to have some upgrades for work that you could buy.
- The game overstays it’s welcome. I think this game is way too long and drags on especially with the home missions where you have to find data to sell. At first they were alright but it got really tedious once you had to balance between 3 sellers. I didn’t do the home missions for money, more so I did them to keep the relationship between the sellers high and not get a game over. I think what would’ve been better is to have the main story be shorter and make an endless mode for those who want more. 
- Unfulfilled promises. I certainly think this is one of the biggest disappointments. Once I learned this game was made possible by kickstarter, I went to its page and saw that the only stretch goals implemented were a series of missions like taking down a cult, finding stolen artifacts, rigging an election etc. The ones that would’ve been really nice like better customization, clearance level 0 and arcade mode were never implemented despite being reached. I also saw comments from the dev saying they are working on a spin-off for this game but that was back in 2020 and their social media hasn’t had a post since then which leads me to believe they’ve abandoned plans altogether which is a big shame.

This is not an easy game nor a polished one. I sense the direction of this game was focused towards a giant sandbox of snooping and somewhere along its devcycle someone said, "Hey, this isn't a game." Then someone else said, “Okay, we have all these things the player can do. Read emails, check contacts. Put people on watchlists… How do we make this into a game?” 

The answer of course was to have the player click on links, clicking on the right ones giving  the player points, or if they got it wrong taking points away. But that was too simple, and not very fun, so they added a couple tools to click on the links in different ways and it made it better. And the Devs (who by this point knew exactly how to use each different link clicking tools) said, “Behold! Fun!” And that’s probably as far as playtesting ever got; to the point where the small team of developers had fun playing their own game. 

This is always a problem with small indies with big visions,  they didn’t have time to playtest and get substantitive player feedback. And the biggest problem this game actually has is that the player doesn't receive feedback until  they’ve already failed. Of course, you can review these mistakes after you've failed, but with all the data you need to take in, it is difficult to parse exactly what you did wrong or even how you failed in some cases.

Despite these problems,  this game has there is a good core gameplay loop and a pretty fascinating story. KtK is a competent game in many senses and does not deserved to be tossed aside as a bad game when it is simly missing satisfying feedback.

With time I imagine this game’s player feedback will be fixed. And if it ever is, I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone with an interest in "connect the dots" style gameplay and Snowden Era cyberspying.  Right now, the only people I would recommend it to are people who not only love the genre and click on the right thing mechanics, but also have a high tolerance for failing and vigorously studying their failures and don't mind reading forum posts to figure stuff out.

Edit for patches: The developers have accomplished a lot in making the early gameplay more intelligible.

I do enjoy the game so far but have not ventured too far down the rabbit hole. It does remind me of Papers Please, Orwell and such, which if you are into, this should be right up your alley. This game requires a lot of my concentration, due to spotting tiny differences like spelling mistakes, timing of phone calls instead of just the contact person etc. It's not necessarily a bad thing, but I can't play it for too long as I would feel mentally tired after a while. It's a fun game I pop into for a couple sessions and then hop out of, and not something I can play all night and feel relaxed. 

All in all I would recommend if you enjoy this genre, and I did feel like I was making a difference with my "work", I guess. My main gripe is something lot of other reviews have mentioned, that the game was marketed as a game of choice, so you could choose to use your "powers" for good or evil, choose how you handle the information and what side you are on etc. However, this is not truly the case because you end up having to balance all the different "sides" to avoid a game over. This feels incongruent with the marketing and does not feel too nice when you realize you have to play all the sides, essentially lying to everyone, and cannot really play the game the way you want to, or that your character would have. The storyline is pretty linear so far, which also does not match my expectation of the game and I've been following it's development from way back.

Other than that, it's an interesting take on the surveillance topic. Wish there was an easier mode for when I want to chill out, or a creative mode that does not force me to make a choice I do not want to, is all.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What is this game?[/h1]
It is the foremost NSA-watch-the-world-from-an-office simulator you will find as of the time of writing this review, and possibly for a long time.

You play a young man, joining a government agency. The rabbithole goes deep, and you are thrusted into a position of Orwellian surveillance, intrigue and thrill.

Starting at the bottom, you analyze simple things. Metadata, browser history and try to piece together a puzzle that is very clearly Need To Know. Given only slight glimpses of what is truly going on in this world. As you progress, you will advance in rank, getting a higher and higher level of clearance, and quickly find yourself face to face with the choice of whether or not to use your access for the good of the agency, the government, the country. the people or even yourself. 

Utilizing your powers of cyber-espionage to predict and even outright uncover your flings interests and hobbies, getting the IRS to get off your back, finding your sister/brother during an emergency or even getting out of paying your rent.

It very quickly becomes apparent what kind of power it actually is you are trusted with, and you will immediately realize why exactly it is so dangerous if left unchecked.

Don't just take it from me. Take it from the very person who knows this the best when he retweeted the game
[i]"Art imitates life."
~Edward Snowden[/i]

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The graphic artstyle of this game is great. It's minimalistic, but still detailed in the way it is done. The whole layout gives a sense of a point-and-click adventure, and for all intents and purposes it is.

Graphically, this game is unique in the way it focuses on the mechanics and uses the art direction to enhance them. You're never distracted by what's on the screen or in your peripheral vision, yet even after many hours (I'm writing this after a 24 hour bender on this game) it never ceases to be interesting or captivating. Artistically, it's very clear it was drawn by somebody who is passionate about the game, and it shows.

[h1]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h1]
The game had a very rough start at launch, with virtually no tutorial. That has been corrected. The team behind this game are very active both on the games own Subreddit, taking into account all the reports being thrown at them and have now rolled out the fourth daily patch in a row. Where else do you see that?

The gameplay itself is good. However, I will be the first to admit that it can be un-intuitive. They have and still are taking steps to improve on this, but the game itself doesn't suffer that heavily under the previous or current issues. It plays like one would very much expect of a game of this type, yet it manages to do [i]so much[/i] with the established fundamentals of the game. Despite having pre-ordered this the moment I saw it almost half a year ago (it has been in development since 2016 and undergone many redesigns), I was honestly afraid that it would end up like most games of this caliber do, where you end up feeling the developers grasping at straws, and the game for its breath as it tries to reskin the same old mechanics and play them off as changes to the gameplay. The gameplay [b]does not change[/b], and thats strangely enough the charm and appeal.

Connect the dots as you chain together events from mere fragments of information such as e-mails, texts, social media, phone calls, browser history, bank account transcripts and decide the fate of the very people you've been spying on from behind your screen. Will you label them a threat for speaking their mind in, what they assumed to be total privacy and confidence, or will you stand up and become a whistleblower and help bring down this omniscient, omnipotent government entity?

You do unlock new abilities progressively as you pass through the ranks of this fictional quasi-NSA government agency, but they do not change the way the game plays, only improve and enhance upon it. All too often do you see games desperately trying to change its own formula throughout the span of the game, and it more often than not ends up sweeping the rug out from under themselves. You won't find that here.

I have never been much for point-and-click games. So much so that I own none except for Orwell and Need to Know. If you have played Orwell, you will without a doubt find yourself enamored with this title.

On a final note, I'll add that there is a story. Getting into it here wouldn't do it justice, and I haven't even completed the game yet. But it will draw you in. Seemingly unrelated events tie together into something larger, and as you scale the ranks of this clandestine government, denying counter-surveillance groups information (or perhaps supplying it yourself), so does the plot thicken and grow.

I would most definitely recommend this game to pretty much anybody who likes a captivating experience.

It is not without flaws, but the developers have rolled out daily fixes since release, and are obviously very passionate about this game. It's not early access, but it isn't a triple-A polished and buffed product, either. But it is getting there.

review_text_raw:
Good game for mature children and teens, but most adults will be disappointed. The main game mechanic is "finding a needle in a haystack". Unfortunately, the haystack is tiny, and the needles are not very well hidden. You are provided a list of keywords to find in tiny documents, given basic criteria. The biggest challenge is making sure it is spelled correctly before highlighting it. I expected the game to be more investigatory, being able to follow leads, etc... this is not that kind of game.

Your character is a young adult, fresh out of college, working his/her first job. The story and the style of the dialogue was written to appeal to children. At one point, my friend in the game texts me to ask who was my high school crush. I immediately assume he is phishing for the answer to my security question to hack my password, but no. I'm overthinking. The game just does this to determine if your crush was a male or female, so it can introduce a new character into the game.

The icing on the cake for why I have to give this game a thumbs down... An anti-government group tries to extort me. There is no option to report this to the Department. I choose not to provide them any documents, because I take national security seriously, and then I lose the game. ---You must leak classified documents, or it is game over.

So much for Monomyth Games' "will you stand up for privacy, or help create an unstoppable police state?" ---Well, I'm forced to leak classified documents to terrorists, so I guess I don't have much choice in the matter.

Monomyth Games also writes, "You can also resist ... by aiding underground groups ... Or, you can just use all of that juicy classified information for your own personal gain. Your call." ---But it's not my call, because if you don't leak the classified information, it is game over.

The pitch made about the game misrepresents the actual game. I would have paid twice as much for the game if it delivered on what was promised, but as it is, I feel duped. They did a really good job on the graphics and interface design... moral dilemmas in stories are awesome, but you can't propose a moral dilemma to the player and then force a game over state if they choose to follow federal law.

I'm overthinking. The game just does this to determine if your crush was a male or female, so it can introduce a new character into the game. The icing on the cake for why I have to give this game a thumbs down... An anti-government group tries to extort me. There is no option to report this to the Department. I choose not to provide them any documents, because I take national security seriously, and then I lose the game. ---You must leak classified documents, or it is game over. So much for Monomyth Games' "will you stand up for privacy, or help create an unstoppable police state?" ---Well, I'm forced to leak classified documents to terrorists, so I guess I don't have much choice in the matter. I would have paid twice as much for the game if it delivered on what was promised, but as it is, I feel duped. [b][i]Need to Know[/i][/b] is a surveillance simulation, the gameplay of which is somewhat reminiscent of the cold and  calculated [i]papers, please[/i]. You assume the role of an employee of an NSA-like organization called The Department of Liberty, and take care of checking people's browsing history and other personal information to identify a possible security risk. The game gives you more options and scary ways to control the longer you play and rise in security clearance. There is always an elementary question floating in the room: Do you stand up for individual rights or do you help to create an uncontrollable police state.

With its topics, [b][i]Need to Know[/i][/b] is not only closer to reality than many other games, it also creates a completely new game approach that will involve many moral decisions. The gameplay, which is basically just scanning data and making quick decisions, is very close to the border crossing simulation [i]papers, please[/i]. Nevertheless, since then hardly any studios have dared to deal with a political issue that affects us all in a similarly dry and fascinating way.

- Memorable characters
- Nice story events
- Wonderful atmosphere
- Highly addictive

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Won't appeal to everyone

So I was one of the people who tracked this game from pretty much the start. I backed it because I loved the idea of the setting and the Papers, Please-style gameplay. Now that I've finished the final product I can say I got both a little more and a little less then I anticipated.

So let's start with what was good.


From what I saw this game looked like a 1984-style distopian future game. It seemed like you would play as an evil institution with no goal but to moniter what people think. As it turned out, the game made it much more complicated, in a good way, that is.

The final product had a story far more intriguing then what I expected. As it turns our, the DoL (That's Department of Liberty, the department you work for) Does infringe on the privacy of everyone, but it also stops criminals, terrorists and even helps people deal with a natural disaster at one point. On the other hand the system can also be abused. even by yourself if you so desire. Still, there is acctually a bit of an argument for the work you do in this game. I expected it to be very one-sided but the game proved me wrong.

Aside from that, watching your character change over time, getting richter and with that more morally flexible, is also a lot of fun. As you rise trough the ranks of the game the department also pulls more and more power towards it. The change from the current world to an all-monitoring police state doesn't come instantanious, but slowly, as I imagine it would in reality as well. The story took me about 40 hours to complete.

Lastly, on the list of good things are the suspects. Every one of them has a personal profile and getting and image of who they are by reading through their ever-increasing personal information is also a lot of fun. Without giving to much away, you sometimes get to know stuff about suspects that they don't even know themselves.


Now on to the stuff I expected more from.

So the gameplay looked like it would be very fun. You sort through every suspect and decide if they're dangerous or not. Now this is pretty much what you do, and it starts of being a lot of fun, but the gameplay is very slow to add new elements. It takes very long before the game becomes more challanging. Also maybe it's because I played the game quite intensively, but it got a little boring after a while. To me the gameplay started to feel like a chore near the end. I believe they should have made more variety in the missions by adding more stuff. I tended to stop playing the game when the gameplay got too dull for me. Then after a while I'd go back to it for the story.

There is also the fact that there is no timer. You can take as long as you want to finish your mission. I'm personally a little split on this fact. On the one side, I'm glad you can just take your time. I personally get quite stressed when a game gives you a timelimit and I'm pretty sure I'm not the only one on this. I also like that you can just take your time and learn all about a suspect if you like. It gives you a chance to enjoy all the detailed profiles that are in the game.
On the other side I do feel like not having a time limit makes the game a little easy. Mostly at the beginning you can just do most missions flawlessly because there is no limit to how long you can take reading about a suspect.

So if you're looking for a game with a really intriguing story and are willing to put up with getting bored of the gameplay a little from time to time, I would advise getting this game. The story really is great and it totally made the game worth it for me. If you want to buy this game for the gameplay, maybe try playing the Alpha or Beta version first and see if you would like more of that. And when I say more I mean quite a lot more.

I backed this game on Kickstarter 3 or 4 years ago and forgot about it till now. For 15 dollars (I paid 12), this game has been worth every penny. I really enjoyed the progression of security rankings and the data and power that came along with them. I also liked the ironic naming of the Department of Liberty. The little news headlines were interesting to read and paralleled our society in a way that made me think "Could this be us someday?" 

I don't know if your overall play style affects the endgame but I chose to play as a ruthless arm of the state just to see how far I could take my power. In the end, I chose to [spoiler] become the new director of the all powerful DoL and take down Charles Douglas. [/spoiler] However, in real life I found myself disgusted at the choices I "had" to make in the name of security and personal gain. Just knowing that I was violating privacy AND potentially ruining lives was quite the experience. The people I betrayed and killed felt real and conflicting. But alas, [strike] control [/strike] ... I mean security above all else, no?

The game can be played all through a mouse. A couple times my CODEX world-map background refused to pop up until I clicked it or tried to scroll. The biometric data was a little graphically glitchy. A few times I was confused at new task assignment types but I figured it out. Overall, a polished game with little complaints especially for how affordable it is. 

It felt rewarding to see Clearance Level 1, Rank = 1st. The soundtrack was [b] beautiful, [/b] truly well composed. The game made me feel conflict and emotion which is indicative of an excellent work of media/art/etc. If you are interested in surveillance, politics, culture, RPG's, or conflict this game is for you. After my play-through, I can't help to reflect on our own society and how much this game may or may not be representative of our current (and future) society. Excellent job Monomyth Games, kudos for this excellent game!

I loved this game. Recommend.

Selling point:
The morally ambigious writing and the logical characters. The game makes you feel you are part of a 90s political thriller, set in the modern world.

Pros:
- writing is amazing
- puzzles are logical and set in the real world
- aesthetics are minimalistic, but cool (my only gripe is that some people looked bizarre),
- game duration (game changes pace once it gets slightly repetitive, which was welcome)
- world-building (despite its conspiracy context, the game is very much grounded in the real world both in terms of politics and technology, and everything felt contemporary, even in its future years)
- achievements (100% completion is based on completing the game, not on some wild goose chase)

Cons:
- UI (common visual glitches, although I do play on linux which may add glitches; animations are slow, changing suspects is slow, link puzzles between multiple suspects are slow not due to complexity of puzzle but due to UI problems; clicking on suspects is difficult even if you remove map scrolling)
- some puzzle solutions have obtuse or small consequences, could have kept its linearity but with some more impact on world, you do get some comics balloons for some optional objectives
- game does push you to become a government bot, even if your character disagrees wildly with that (but this is somewhat necessary from a writing standpoint).

In Brief:
This is a very good game for someone who is interested in mass surveillance, abuse of power, corporate capitalism, world politics, solving puzzles, and in general feeling like a special part of an important conspiracy.
